questions.prompt: You pushed a feature branch and a teammate pulled it. Now you rebase that branch onto main and force-push. What goes wrong for the teammate?
options: Nothing — force-push replaces the branch and their next pull reconciles it
Their existing commits and your rebased ones are different objects with the same changes, so merging both applies the work twice
Their local branch is deleted when they pull
The force-push is rejected because the branch has a merge commit
questions.explanation: Rebase gives your commits new parents, so new hashes — while their copy keeps the old ones. Neither git nor the merge machinery knows they are the same change, so a merge of both branches applies it twice. Force-push replacing a branch (A) is exactly the failure: it discards what they had without merging it. Local branches are not deleted by a remote force-push (C), and the push is accepted, not rejected (D).

questions.prompt: git merge main on your branch reports 'Fast-forward'. What does that tell you?
options: main had no commits your branch did not already contain, so your label slid forward with no merge commit
main was fully merged into your branch with a merge commit
Your branch was fast-forwarded to a remote copy of main
The merge was trivial because the branches touched disjoint files
questions.explanation: Fast-forward is specifically the no-join case: one line has no commits the other lacks, so there is nothing to record and no merge commit is created. A merge commit (B) is the opposite outcome. Remote copies are a different concept entirely (C) — Lesson 18. And touching disjoint files (D) is a real thing that helps, but it does not prevent a merge commit when both lines have new commits.

questions.prompt: You started pulling and the merge it triggered made a mess of your history. Which reason is the one the lesson says to act on?
options: git pull always merges; pick the variant explicitly with --rebase or --no-rebase so the choice is yours
git pull should be configured once in .gitconfig and never thought about again
Only rebase is safe on a shared branch, merge should never be used
The mess is unavoidable; the fix is a larger --force flag on push
questions.explanation: `pull` is `fetch` plus a join, and the join is the part you should choose out loud. Setting it globally (B) moves the decision somewhere you will forget you made — the same class of bug as letting the default decide. The lesson's rule is directional, not absolute: rebase what you own, merge what others have (C). And force-pushing over it (D) makes the history worse, not the collaboration.

questions.prompt: A rebase finished and the result is wrong. You have not pushed. What gets the old commits back?
options: git rebase --abort, which rewinds the already-finished rebase
git revert, which adds a commit undoing the rebase
The reflog still records where HEAD was before the rebase, so you can reset back to it
Nothing — once a rebase completes, the original commits no longer exist
questions.explanation: A rebase moves labels and creates new commits; it deletes nothing, so every prior HEAD position is still in the reflog. `--abort` only applies while the rebase is still running (A). `revert` adds an undo commit on top, which leaves the rebased history in place — a different goal (B). And the originals are emphatically still there (C's neighbour D) — that is why rebasing an unpushed branch is safe enough to recommend.
